job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Olga Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I wake up around eight in the room I share with my friend Dana in Nottingham, and I'm on the job boards by nine. I've sent sixty-one applications for junior mechanical roles since June and got three automated rejections and silence from the rest. Two days a week I do cash shifts at a garden centre, and the rest of the day I rewrite my CV for the fourth time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what was your final project?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mechanical engineering at a university in the Midlands, with a pass degree. My final project was redesigning a pump housing so it cost less to cast, and our group scraped a pass because one member vanished before the report was due. I had no placement year, and every job ad seems to ask for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the garden centre I'd say it's the same old story: big promises, nothing for people like me. To friends I'd say the hype is mostly shareholders talking. Online I'd probably say nothing, because I don't like arguing with strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my problem stays exactly what it is now. Nothing about AI fixes the real problem: too many graduates, too few junior jobs, and companies who'd rather hire nobody than train somebody. I'm still the one with the debt and no offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, maybe ten a week instead of five, and ask my university careers office for the alumni list again. I'd try to get the garden centre up to four days. If nothing comes by spring I'd look at the council's graduate scheme, even though the pay is low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It's a relief that nothing dramatic happens, but it isn't real calm, because rent is due on the first and the garden centre can cut my hours in winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd say nothing online. What holds you back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year I posted that graduate schemes favour people with connections, and a man I'd never met told me to learn to code properly. I deleted it. I'm tired of being told my situation is my own fault when the figures say otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if the garden centre drops your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My phone plan, then the bus pass, so I'd walk forty minutes to interviews. Food is already rice and lentils. Dana would wait a couple of weeks for rent, but I'd go to the food bank before asking anyone else.

say: I'd tell colleagues at the garden centre that **AI hype** is mostly shareholders talking.
I wouldn't post online; strangers just tell graduates to try harder.
To friends I'd say **nothing changes** for people like me.
think: The real problem is **too few junior jobs**, and AI doesn't touch that.
Employers would rather hire nobody than train a graduate, and my **debt** stays the same.
do: Send **ten applications** a week instead of five.
Ask the careers office for the alumni list and ask for **four shifts** at the garden centre.
Look at the council graduate scheme by spring if nothing comes.
feel: Tired, with only a thin relief that nothing dramatic happens.
Worried about **winter hours** and rent, so the calm isn't real.
S0.quote: Nothing about AI fixes the real problem: too many graduates, too few junior jobs, and companies who'd rather hire nobody than train somebody.
fieldNote: Her worry comes from the **job market** and debt, not from AI itself.
Angry at **employers** and at people who blame graduates.
Small, practical plans; no plan beyond the council scheme.

steps.text: Send ten job applications a week instead of five
Apply to the council graduate scheme if nothing comes by spring
Drop the phone plan and walk to interviews

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's another way for firms to get thinking work done without paying a person. At the garden centre they'd laugh, but my friends in computing say entry-level coding roles are already vanishing. Online, I'd back anyone calling for rules on how firms use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the junior jobs I'm applying for are exactly the ones that go first. A company that used to hire three graduates to check drawings and write reports will hire one, or none. Junior jobs checking drawings and writing reports will go first, and I'm at the back of the graduate job queue with a pass degree and no placement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably join the graduate section of a union, because I'd want someone speaking for people like me. I'd keep applying, and I'd widen it to technician jobs in factories, where somebody still has to touch the machine. I still wouldn't touch the AI tools, though I know that counts against me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, more than scared. I keep seeing companies announce record profits and a hiring freeze in the same week. Scared comes at night, when I do the sums on my loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't use the AI tools. What's behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I tried one once for a cover letter and it wrote the same smooth rubbish everyone else got. I don't trust it, and I don't want to train my own replacement. Maybe that's stubborn, but I'd rather be slow and honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a union actually do for someone who hasn't got a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much on day one, I know. But it can push for graduate jobs to be advertised properly, and for firms to pay people on trial periods. At least I'd be in a room where it's discussed instead of shouting at my screen.

say: I'd say firms use AI to get **thinking work** done without paying a person.
Online I'd back rules on how companies can use it.
I'd tell friends the **union route** is the only way graduates get heard.
think: Junior drawing-check and report jobs go first, and I'm at the back of the queue.
A **pass degree** with no placement makes me easy to skip.
do: Join a **graduate union** section and keep applying.
Widen the search to **technician jobs** in factories.
Stay away from AI tools, even if that counts against me.
feel: Angry at record profits alongside hiring freezes.
Scared at night when I do the **loan sums**.
S1.quote: Junior jobs checking drawings and writing reports will go first, and I'm at the back of the graduate job queue with a pass degree and no placement.
fieldNote: Blames **employers** and wants a collective voice; not looking to adapt herself.
Refuses **AI tools** on principle, which she half-admits hurts her.
Widening to **technician work** shows flexibility on jobs, none on tools.

steps.text: Join the graduate section of an engineering union
Apply for factory technician jobs within an hour's bus ride
Keep sending applications and avoid AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is a crime against people my age. Governments are asleep. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen, at the garden centre, to Dana, and in the comments of every news story I read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means my degree is worth nothing before I've even used it. Thinking work is what I trained for, and if that's gone by 2028 then the jobs I've been chasing never come back. The robots arrive later for hands-on work, but I've no hands-on skills to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop applying for anything that looks like desk engineering and look for an electrician or maintenance apprenticeship that takes graduates. I'd keep every hour at the garden centre and ask for more. And I'd go to a protest, I've never been to one, but I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, scared stiff. I can't see how I make a plan in two years with debt and under a month of savings. My future feels like the floor is going while I'm still looking for the stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to happen in those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the government to say plainly what happens to people who can't get work: paid retraining, pausing student loan repayments, something. Right now no one says anything. Two years is not enough time to retrain a whole generation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dana that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dana we should stay in the flat and pool every pound. Dana works at a call centre, which will go even earlier than my job hunt. We'd sit at the kitchen table and write out what we could cut, and neither of us would sleep.

say: I'd call two years **a crime** against people my age.
I'd say governments are asleep and say it loudly, at work and online.
think: My degree is **worth nothing** before I've used it.
I have no hands-on skills to fall back on, and under a month of savings.
do: Look for **maintenance or electrician apprenticeships** that take graduates.
Take every garden centre hour and go to a **protest** for the first time.
Pool money with Dana and write out every cost we can cut.
feel: **Scared stiff**, like the floor is going while I look for the stairs.
Powerless: I can't see a plan within two years.
S2.quote: My future feels like the floor is going while I'm still looking for the stairs.
fieldNote: Her **thin cushion** leaves her with no plan at all here.
Reaches for collective action and **public support** because she has no buffer.
Friend Dana's **call centre** job is a second pressure she names.

steps.text: Apply for maintenance and electrician apprenticeships that accept graduates
Go to a protest about jobs and AI
Pool rent money with Dana and write a list of cuts
Ask the council what retraining help exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two, but I'd still say it's too fast. I'd say we need laws in place now: retraining paid for by the companies that profit, and graduate jobs protected for a while. I'd put that on whatever petition was going round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years gives me a chance if I move quickly, but not if I stay stuck the way I am now. If I find any job in the next year, I might build enough of a record to survive until 2031. If I don't, I'm just a pass degree from the old world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first technician or maintenance job offered and not wait for a perfect graduate role. I'd save a bit each month, even thirty pounds, and start a part-time course in electrical installation at the college. I'd also vote for whoever promised retraining money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit calmer than the two-year one, because I can picture steps. But the debt is still there, and I'd be afraid the steps are all too small and too slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change for you, compared with 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can pay for a trade qualification and still be young enough to use it. In two years I'd be in the same hole. Five years is time to be hands-on before the robots arrive in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if you got a job next spring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in it even if it was boring, and I'd keep the garden centre shifts for a few months to build savings. Last year I'd have chased a better offer. Now a job is something I'd hold on to with both hands.

say: I'd say we need **laws now**: companies that profit should pay for retraining.
I'd sign any petition that protects graduate jobs for a while.
think: Five years gives me a chance if I **move quickly**.
If I stay unemployed, I'm a pass degree from the old world.
do: Take the first **technician job** offered, not wait for a perfect role.
Save **thirty pounds** a month and start an evening electrical course.
Vote for whoever promises retraining money.
feel: Calmer than 2028, because I can picture steps.
Still afraid the steps are **too small** and too slow.
S3.quote: In two years I'd be in the same hole. Five years is time to be hands-on before the robots arrive in 2034.
fieldNote: The longer warning lets her think about **trades**, and she says so.
Still no savings, so every plan depends on landing **any job** first.
She talks about **voting** and lobbying more than in other scenarios.

steps.text: Accept the first technician or maintenance job offered
Enrol in an evening electrical installation course at the college
Put thirty pounds a month into a savings account
Vote for the party promising paid retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds like a long time, so I'd say fine, we have a decade, so use it properly. I'd say that to young people especially: don't panic, but organise. Every year spent without rules is a year wasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years is enough for me to get out of debt, if I find work. I'd be 33 by 2036, which isn't old. I could change career at least once, maybe train as a surveyor or a lift engineer, something with a physical side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd find any steady job first and pay the debt down hard. I'd go back to evening classes for a trade in about two years. And I'd keep going to union meetings, because ten years of nothing from the government would make me angrier than ten months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay, even a bit hopeful. It's the only one where I imagine a normal life, a flat of my own, maybe a dog. I know that could be false comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it could be false comfort. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is also long enough for the government to do nothing. If nobody prepares, we'd reach 2036 with the same debt and the same companies. I'm only calm if people like me push and somebody listens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in year one specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one is just getting a job, any job near Nottingham, and paying two hundred a month off the loan. Year two is the evening course. I'd write the dates in my diary so it's not a vague hope.

say: I'd tell young people: don't panic, but **organise**.
A decade is long enough, so every year without rules is wasted.
think: Ten years is enough to clear debt, if I find **steady work**.
I'd be 33 in 2036, young enough to change career once.
do: Find any **steady job** and pay two hundred a month off the loan.
Start evening trade classes in about **two years**.
Keep going to union meetings and write the dates in my diary.
feel: Mostly okay and a bit hopeful, picturing a flat of my own.
Aware this might be **false comfort** if nobody prepares.
S4.quote: Ten years is also long enough for the government to do nothing.
fieldNote: Her only scenario with a **normal life** in view; hope still hangs on a first job.
Trust in government is low, so calm depends on **pressure** from below.
Specific **dates** and amounts make this her most concrete plan.

steps.text: Take any steady job near Nottingham within the year
Pay two hundred a month off the student loan
Start evening classes in a hands-on trade in two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. I'd have no time and no money to make a plan, and people like me would be told it's our fault. What would help is a government that said openly what it would do, paid retraining, a pause on loan repayments, and firms that have to hire and train graduates for a few years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people think graduates are privileged, and I'm not. I'm washing pots at a garden centre with an engineering degree. Nobody should have to carry forty thousand of debt and a pass degree into this.

headlineQuote: I'm washing pots at a garden centre with an engineering degree. Nobody should have to carry forty thousand of debt and a pass degree into this.
portrait: **Olga**, 23, finished mechanical engineering with a pass, no placement, and shares a room in Nottingham with her friend Dana.
She has about **sixty applications** out, cash shifts at a garden centre and heavy student debt.
Left-leaning and angry at employers and government, she trusts **unions** and rules more than tools.
She never uses AI and is slow to change, so she leans on a **first job**, a trade course and group action.
Her mood ranges from panic in the two-year world to cautious hope in the ten-year world.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world worries her most: no time, no money and no plan.
She fears graduates will be blamed for what happens to them.
whatWouldHelp: A government that states a plan: **paid retraining** and a pause on loan repayments.
Firms required to hire and train **graduates** for a few years.
